title: integrable_3d_zx_y — Compact Box to Ioc Product
content:
`integrable_3d_zx_y` proves that G((z,x),y) = f(x,y,z) is integrable on the triple Ioc product measure. The proof chain: (1) G is continuous (composition of f with a coordinate permutation); (2) G is integrableOn the compact Icc box [e,f']×[a,b]×[c,d]; (3) Two applications of restrict_prod_eq_prod_restrict convert Icc to an Icc product measure; (4) mono_set transfers from Icc to Ioc (since Ioc ⊆ Icc). The permutation of arguments ((z,x),y) ↦ f(x,y,z) is what enables the outer integral swap in Step 2.

The sibling lemma `integrable_3d_xy_z` (line 91) follows the identical pattern but with the rearrangement ((x,y),z) ↦ f(x,y,z), powering the (y,x,z) ↔ (x,y,z) swap in `triple_fubini_yxz_eq_xyz`.
mathContext:
For $f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ continuous, the function $G: ((z,x), y) \mapsto f(x,y,z)$ is integrable on the product measure $\mu_{(e,f']} \otimes \mu_{(a,b]} \otimes \mu_{(c,d]}$ (where $\mu_{(p,q]}$ is Lebesgue measure restricted to the half-open interval $(p,q]$). Key chain: continuity of $G$ + compactness of the closed box $[e,f'] \times [a,b] \times [c,d]$ ⟹ $G$ integrable on the closed box ⟹ (via `mono_set`, since $(p,q] \subset [p,q]$) $G$ integrable on the half-open box ⟹ (via `Measure.prod_restrict`) $G$ integrable on the product of restricted measures.

This structural lemma is then fed to `Integrable.integral_prod_right`: if $G$ is integrable on $\mu \otimes \nu$, then $(p \mapsto \int_{\nu} G(p, \cdot))$ is integrable on $\mu$. Applied to the 3D product, this gives integrability of $(z,x) \mapsto \int_y f(x,y,z)$, which is exactly what `MeasureTheory.integral_integral_swap` requires.

title: triple_fubini_of_continuous — 3-Step Transposition
content:
`triple_fubini_of_continuous` proves ∫z∫y∫x f = ∫x∫y∫z f via three steps:
1. **Step 1** (lines 136-141): For each fixed z, swap (x,y) using the parent theorem `GreensTheoremOQ01OQ01.fubini_of_continuous` — this is a pointwise application using `intervalIntegral.integral_congr`. The continuity of $(x,y) \mapsto f(x,y,z)$ is recovered by `hf.comp` with the projection that fixes z.
2. **Step 2** (lines 143-147): Swap the outer (z,x) pair using `MeasureTheory.integral_integral_swap`. This requires converting `intervalIntegral` to set integrals via `integral_of_le`, then verifying the parameterized integrability hypothesis: `(integrable_3d_zx_y hf …).integral_prod_left` extracts integrability of $(z,x) \mapsto \int_y f(x,y,z)$ from 3D integrability via `integral_prod_left`.
3. **Step 3** (lines 149-154): Symmetric to Step 1 — for each fixed x, swap (y,z) via 2D Fubini.

The three steps are then composed by `rw [step1, step2, step3]`. This is the heart of the 3D Fubini bridge and is the model for the n-D recursion.
mathContext:
The 3-step proof: let $I_{zyx} = \int_z \int_y \int_x f$. (1) By 2D Fubini under $z$: $I_{zyx} = \int_z \int_x \int_y f = I_{zxy}$. (2) By `integral_integral_swap` ($\int_z \int_x h = \int_x \int_z h$ for integrable $h$): $I_{zxy} = I_{xzy}$. (3) By 2D Fubini under $x$: $I_{xzy} = \int_x \int_y \int_z f = I_{xyz}$. The key technical requirement for step (2) is: $(z,x) \mapsto \int_y f(x,y,z)$ is integrable on $\mu_z \otimes \mu_x$ — provided by `integrable_3d_zx_y.integral_prod_left`.

Observe that the cycle $(zyx) \to (zxy) \to (xzy) \to (xyz)$ involves transpositions $(xy)$, $(zx)$, $(yz)$ — the three adjacent transpositions of $S_3$, which together generate all of $S_3$. This pattern (peel off the outer integral, recurse with one less variable, then use a single outer transposition) is exactly the structure that lifts to general $n$ via `Equiv.Perm.swap_induction_on` in the subsidiary module.

title: triple_fubini_yxz_eq_xyz — The (y,x) Outer Swap
content:
`triple_fubini_yxz_eq_xyz` proves ∫y∫x∫z f = ∫x∫y∫z f, complementing `triple_fubini_of_continuous` (which handles the (z,y,x) → (x,y,z) cycle). The proof:
1. Convert `intervalIntegral` to set integrals via `integral_of_le hab/hcd/hef`.
2. Apply `symm` to flip the equation, then `MeasureTheory.integral_integral_swap` (which proves $\int x \int y = \int y \int x$). After `symm`, the goal matches.
3. Discharge the integrability hypothesis with `(integrable_3d_xy_z hf …).integral_prod_left`, which produces integrability of $(x,y) \mapsto \int_z f(x,y,z)$ on the 2D Ioc product.

This lemma is what allows `triple_fubini_all_equal` to cover *all* outer-variable orderings: triple_fubini_of_continuous handles (z,y,x) → (x,y,z); the (z,x,y) → (x,y,z) case is reduced to triple_fubini_of_continuous via a 2D Fubini under z; and (y,x,z) → (x,y,z) is exactly this lemma.
mathContext:
The 6 permutations of $(x,y,z)$ form $S_3$. Three are obtained by varying which variable is innermost: (x,y,z), (z,x,y), (y,z,x). The other three flip a pair: (y,x,z), (x,z,y), (z,y,x). The earlier `triple_fubini_of_continuous` swaps two innermost variables together with an outer swap (a 3-cycle); this lemma handles the simple 2-transposition $(x,y)$ on the *outermost* two variables.

The trick: at this point the innermost integral $\int_z$ is fixed in both sides, so we are reduced to proving $\int_y \int_x g = \int_x \int_y g$ for $g(x,y) = \int_z f(x,y,z)$. This is just 2D Fubini for $g$, but proved here via `integral_integral_swap` (the abstract product-measure form) with integrability supplied by `integrable_3d_xy_z.integral_prod_left`.

title: triple_fubini_all_equal — Three Generators Cover S₃
content: `triple_fubini_all_equal` proves that three key orderings of ∫∫∫ f all equal the canonical (x,y,z) ordering. The proof is a straightforward composition: (z,y,x) = (x,y,z) is `triple_fubini_of_continuous`; (z,x,y) = (x,y,z) by first using 2D Fubini inside (reverse) then `triple_fubini_of_continuous`; (y,x,z) = (x,y,z) is `triple_fubini_yxz_eq_xyz`. Together these generators (transpositions (1 2), (1 3), (2 3) modulo composition) suffice to generate all 3! = 6 permutations of 3 variables.
mathContext: The symmetric group $S_3$ is generated by the adjacent transpositions $(12)$, $(23)$, and $(13)$: the three generators $\tau_{zyx \to xyz}$, $\tau_{zxy \to xyz}$, $\tau_{yxz \to xyz}$ established here correspond to compositions of these transpositions. Since $|S_3| = 6$ and any permutation of 3 elements can be written as a product of at most 3 transpositions, these three theorems (plus symmetry of `=`) give all 6 orderings. For $n > 3$, the pattern generalizes inductively via `Equiv.Perm.swap_induction_on`: any $\sigma \in S_n$ decomposes into adjacent swaps, and each adjacent swap is handled by an (integral_integral_swap)-style argument inside the iterated integral.

title: iteratedIntervalIntegral — The n-Dimensional Recursion
content:
The n-fold iterated interval integral is defined by recursion on n:
- **Base case (n=0)**: returns f applied to the empty function `Fin.elim0`.
- **Inductive case (n=k+1)**: integrates the outermost variable x₀ from a(0) to b(0) and recurses on the remaining variables via `Fin.tail`.

The four auxiliary lemmas prove the n=0, n=1, n=2 cases explicitly:
- `iteratedIntervalIntegral_zero`: base case (just `rfl`).
- `iteratedIntervalIntegral_succ`: the recursive unfolding equation.
- `iteratedIntervalIntegral_one`: n=1 reduces to a single `intervalIntegral`.
- `iteratedIntervalIntegral_two`: n=2 reduces to ∫x∫y f, recovering the 2D Fubini setup.

The `@[simp]` attribute on the base/successor cases makes these lemmas automatically unfold during proof normalisation, reducing iterated-integral expressions to nested intervalIntegral calls that can be combined with `triple_fubini_*` results for n≤3 or with the order-independence theorem from the subsidiary module for general n.
mathContext:
Formal definition by structural recursion on $n$: $$\mathcal{I}_{a,b}[f] = \begin{cases} f(\emptyset) & n = 0 \\ \int_{a_0}^{b_0} \mathcal{I}_{\text{tail}(a), \text{tail}(b)}[x' \mapsto f(x_0 :: x')]\, dx_0 & n = k+1 \end{cases}$$ where `Fin.tail a : Fin k → ℝ` drops the first component of $a : \text{Fin}(k+1) \to \mathbb{R}$, and `Fin.cons x x' : Fin (k+1) → ℝ` prepends $x_0$. This produces the iterated integral $\int_{a_0}^{b_0} \int_{a_1}^{b_1} \cdots \int_{a_{n-1}}^{b_{n-1}} f(x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1})\, dx_{n-1} \cdots dx_0$.

This definition is `noncomputable` because `intervalIntegral` is itself noncomputable (Bochner integration is defined via simple-function approximation, not by elementary means). Formalizing iterated integrals over `Fin n` rather than via curried function types makes order-of-integration arguments expressible as permutations $\sigma \in S_n$ rather than as informal claims about "swapping the order of integration".

title: N-Dimensional Order Independence — Axiom Retired
content:
**The previously-stated axiom `iteratedIntervalIntegral_order_independent` has been retired.** A first-principles proof for arbitrary $n$ now lives in the subsidiary module `Proofs.GreensTheoremOQ01OQ01OQ01OQ01`, using `Equiv.Perm.swap_induction_on` plus an adjacent-swap Fubini lemma. The 2D and 3D special cases continue to be proved here directly: `fubini_n2` (lines 203-206) handles n=2 by appeal to the parent module, and `triple_fubini_of_continuous` / `triple_fubini_yxz_eq_xyz` together cover n=3.

**Status verification**: this file declares 0 axioms and 0 sorries. The general n-D order-independence theorem in the subsidiary module is also axiom-free: it reduces an arbitrary permutation $\sigma \in S_n$ to a product of adjacent transpositions (`Equiv.Perm.swap_induction_on`), each of which is then dispatched by an `integral_integral_swap`-style argument applied at the appropriate depth in the iterated-integral recursion.
mathContext:
The general theorem (in subsidiary module): for continuous $f : (\mathbb{R}^n) \to \mathbb{R}$ and any permutation $\sigma \in S_n$, $$\mathcal{I}_{a,b}[f] = \mathcal{I}_{a \circ \sigma, b \circ \sigma}[x \mapsto f(x \circ \sigma^{-1})].$$ This says: integrating in the permuted order $(x_{\sigma(0)}, \ldots, x_{\sigma(n-1)})$ gives the same result. Strategy: $S_n$ is generated by adjacent transpositions $(i, i+1)$; an adjacent swap inside the iterated integral is just $\int_{x_i} \int_{x_{i+1}} = \int_{x_{i+1}} \int_{x_i}$, a Fubini swap at depth $i$ inside the recursion; and `Equiv.Perm.swap_induction_on` (Mathlib's standard induction principle on permutations) reduces an arbitrary $\sigma$ to a finite chain of such adjacent swaps.

**Historical note**: in earlier drafts of this file the theorem was stated as an `axiom` to defer the inductive proof. The current version (post-2026-05-06) eliminates this axiom — the entry is now genuinely `verified` (badge: `verified`, axiomCount: 0), demonstrating that the abstract permutation-group induction is tractable in Lean 4 with the current Mathlib infrastructure.
